tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 2. Thermodynamics of Conversion. In 1824 a 28-year-old French military engineer, Sadi Carnot, paid to print 600 copies of a 118-page booklet, Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu. Hardly anyone read it, and Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36. His booklet nonetheless contained an idea that every power plant still obeys: the work you can get from heat is limited by the temperatures between which the heat flows. Almost two centuries later, in March 2018, Guinness World Records recognized Chubu Electric’s Nishi-Nagoya Block 1 in Japan, built around GE 7HA gas turbines, as the world’s most efficient combined-cycle power plant, at 63.08 percent gross efficiency. That plant still sends more than a third of its fuel energy into the air and cooling water. This chapter explains why it must, and why it loses so little compared with the plants that came before it. Chapter 1 showed that a large share of primary energy never becomes a useful service, and that most of the “rejected energy” in a Sankey diagram leaves from thermal power plants. This chapter explains that loss from first principles. Section 2.1 sets out the first and second laws, entropy and exergy, the tools for deciding which losses are inevitable and which are engineering choices. Section 2.2 derives the Carnot limit and compares it with real fleet efficiencies. Section 2.3 analyzes the two workhorse cycles, Rankine (steam) and Brayton (gas turbine), with real operating numbers. Section 2.4 combines them into the combined-cycle gas plant, one of our running examples, and asks when cogeneration makes sense. Chapter 4 uses these results for coal, gas and nuclear plants; Chapters 5 and 6 meet converters, such as wind turbines and fuel cells, that are not heat engines and face different limits.

tracks.label: 2.1 The first and second laws
tracks.text: Section 2 point 1. The first and second laws. Chapter 1 drew energy flows as Sankey diagrams in which every joule entering an economy reappears as a service or as rejected energy. That accounting rests on the first law of thermodynamics: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted. For a closed system the first law reads ΔE = Q minus W, with Q the heat added to the system and W the work it does, both in joules. Power-plant components are better treated as open systems in steady flow. Per kilogram of working fluid, the steady-flow energy equation is q minus w = Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz, where h is the specific enthalpy in kJ/kg. In turbines, pumps and boilers the kinetic and potential energy terms are usually tiny next to Δh, so an adiabatic turbine’s work is simply h_in minus h_out. Steam entering at 3,400 kJ/kg and leaving at 2,300 kJ/kg delivers 1,100 kJ/kg; at a flow of 100 kg/s that is 110,000 kJ/s, or 110 MW. The first law cannot explain the most striking feature of Chapter 1’s Sankey diagrams: fossil and nuclear power plants reject more than half of the energy they take in as low-temperature heat. Energy conservation would be just as happy with a plant that turned all of its fuel into electricity. What forbids that plant is the second law of thermodynamics. Rudolf Clausius, in papers from 1850 onward, built the second law on the observation that heat does not pass by itself from a colder body to a hotter one. The equivalent Kelvin–Planck statement is the one a power engineer meets every day: no device operating in a cycle can take heat from a single reservoir and turn all of it into work. Some heat must always be rejected to a colder body. Section 2.2 shows exactly how much. Clausius gave the quantity behind the second law its name, entropy, in 1865. Entropy S is a property, measured in J/K and defined through reversible heat transfer as dS = δQ_rev/T, with T in kelvin. For any real process the entropy balance is ΔS = ∫δQ/T + S_gen. The entropy generation S_gen is zero for an ideal reversible process and positive for every real one; friction, mixing, combustion and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference all generate entropy. Now apply this to a heat engine. Over one cycle the working fluid returns to its starting state, so its entropy change is zero. The entropy brought in with the heat Q_H at temperature T_H, plus everything generated inside, must leave with the rejected heat: Q_C/T_C = Q_H/T_H + S_gen. Rejected heat is not a design flaw. It is the only exit for entropy. Engineers turn the second law into an accounting tool through exergy: the maximum useful work obtainable from a system or a flow as it comes into equilibrium with its surroundings. The surroundings, called the dead state, are usually taken as T0 = 298.15 K and 101.325 kPa. For a flowing stream the specific flow exergy is ψ = (h minus h0) minus T0(s minus s0) + V²/2 + gz. Heat Q available at temperature T carries exergy Q(1 minus T0/T). A megajoule of heat at 1,500 K is therefore worth 0.80 MJ of work, while a megajoule at 40 degrees Celsius (313 K) is worth only 0.05 MJ. Electricity and shaft work are pure exergy. Unlike energy, exergy is not conserved. The exergy destroyed in any process equals T0·S_gen, a result known as the Gouy–Stodola theorem. The two accountings paint different pictures of the same plant. An energy balance on a coal-fired steam plant shows the largest outflow, more than half the fuel energy, leaving through the condenser into cooling water a few degrees above ambient. An exergy balance shows that this heat was worth little; at 40 degrees Celsius its exergy is under 5 percent of its energy. The largest exergy destruction happens in the boiler, where combustion turns the fuel’s chemical exergy into hot gas, and that gas then gives up its heat across a gap of many hundreds of kelvin to steam. Fuel itself counts as nearly pure exergy, since the chemical exergy of natural gas is close to its heating value. This is why the history of power engineering is a history of raising steam temperatures and, as Section 2.4 shows, of sending high-temperature heat through a gas turbine before it ever reaches steam. A common misconception: Energy is conserved, so a power plant that throws away more than half its fuel energy is just badly engineered; better design could turn nearly all of it into electricity. In fact, The first law allows that, but the second law does not. A cycle that takes in heat must reject enough heat to carry away the entropy that came in, Q_C ≥ Q_H·T_C/T_H. Good engineering reduces the extra entropy generated, but no design removes the rejection itself.

tracks.label: 2.2 The Carnot limit
tracks.text: Section 2 point 2. The Carnot limit. Sadi Carnot published Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu in Paris in 1824, at his own expense, in an edition of 600 copies. He reasoned with the caloric theory of his day, which treated heat as an indestructible fluid, and compared a heat engine with a waterwheel: work comes from caloric “falling” from a high temperature to a low one, as water falls from a high level to a low one. The caloric theory was wrong, but Carnot’s central conclusion survived its overthrow. The maximum work obtainable from heat depends only on the temperatures of the bodies between which it flows, not on the working substance. Émile Clapeyron restated the argument in mathematical form in 1834, and in the early 1850s Clausius and William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, reconciled it with the conservation of energy. The modern derivation takes three lines. An engine takes heat Q_H from a reservoir at T_H, does work W and rejects Q_C to a reservoir at T_C. The first law gives W = Q_H minus Q_C. The entropy balance from Section 2.1 gives Q_C = T_C(Q_H/T_H + S_gen). Substituting, W = Q_H(1 minus T_C/T_H) minus T_C·S_gen. The first term is the most work any engine could deliver; the second is the work lost to irreversibility, and it is never negative. Dividing by Q_H gives the Carnot efficiency, η_C = 1 minus T_C/T_H, reached only by a fully reversible engine with S_gen = 0. Figure 2.1 shows the bookkeeping for steam at 823 K and a condenser at 319 K. The limit is 61 percent, and the ideal steam cycle analyzed in Section 2.3 reaches 41 percent. Both temperatures must be absolute temperatures, in kelvin, because the derivation divides heat by temperature and entropy is measured from absolute zero. The Celsius error is large and common. For steam at 600 degrees Celsius and a condenser at 33 degrees Celsius, 1 minus 33/600 gives an impossible 94.5 percent. The correct value is 1 minus 306.15 K/873.15 K = 0.649, or 64.9 percent. The formula also shows where effort pays. The derivative of η_C with respect to T_H is T_C/T_H², while with respect to T_C it is minus 1/T_H, so a kelvin removed from the cold side is worth more than a kelvin added to the hot side. In practice T_C is pinned near the temperature of the available cooling water or air, so designers push T_H upward until they reach the limits of steels and turbine alloys. Real plants sit well below their Carnot limits. The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes fleet-average heat rates, the fuel energy used per kilowatt-hour generated, on a higher-heating-value basis for fossil fuels (for nuclear plants, the reactor heat). In 2024 they were 10,777 Btu/kWh for coal plants, 10,443 Btu/kWh for nuclear plants and 7,754 Btu/kWh for natural gas plants. Since 1 kWh = 3,412 Btu, the corresponding efficiencies are 3,412/10,777 = 31.7 percent for coal, 3,412/10,443 = 32.7 percent for nuclear and 3,412/7,754 = 44.0 percent for gas. Nuclear plants do only about as well as coal despite a completely different heat source, because light-water reactors raise steam at under 300 degrees Celsius, which keeps T_H low. Gas leads because much of the gas fleet is combined-cycle, the subject of Section 2.4. The gap between real and Carnot efficiency has identifiable causes. A Carnot engine takes in all its heat at T_H and rejects all of it at T_C, with no temperature difference between the working fluid and the reservoirs. A real engine takes in heat over a range of temperatures, needs finite temperature differences to move heat at a useful rate, and loses work to friction and pressure drops. Curzon and Ahlborn showed in 1975 that an engine whose only irreversibility is finite-rate heat transfer, operated for maximum power output, has efficiency 1 minus √(T_C/T_H). For T_H = 873 K and T_C = 306 K that gives 40.8 percent, close to what good steam plants achieve. The Carnot formula is a ceiling, not a forecast. A better measure of engineering quality is the second-law efficiency, η/η_C. A common misconception: No machine can beat the Carnot efficiency, so wind turbines, solar cells and fuel cells must be Carnot-limited too. In fact, The Carnot limit applies to heat engines, devices that turn heat into work. A wind turbine extracts kinetic energy from moving air and is bounded by the Betz limit; a solar cell converts photons and is bounded by the Shockley–Queisser limit (both in Chapter 5). A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly and is bounded by the Gibbs free energy of its reaction, not by any temperature ratio.

tracks.label: 2.3 Rankine and Brayton cycles
tracks.text: Section 2 point 3. Rankine and Brayton cycles. Most of the world’s thermal electricity, from coal, nuclear, geothermal and solar-thermal plants, comes from the Rankine cycle. It is named for William John Macquorn Rankine, Regius Professor of Civil Engineering and Mechanics at Glasgow, whose 1859 Manual of the Steam Engine and Other Prime Movers set out the thermodynamics of steam power for engineers. The ideal cycle has four processes, numbered as in Figure 2.2. From 1 to 2 a pump raises saturated liquid from condenser pressure to boiler pressure. From 2 to 3 the boiler heats, boils and superheats the water at constant pressure. From 3 to 4 the steam expands through a turbine, ideally at constant entropy. From 4 to 1 the condenser turns the wet exhaust back into liquid at constant pressure, rejecting heat to cooling water. The Rankine cycle’s great advantage is the pump. Compressing a liquid takes very little work because its specific volume is tiny, and for an incompressible liquid w_p = v(P2 minus P1). Water at 10 kPa has v = 0.00101 m³/kg, so raising it to 10 MPa takes 0.00101 m³/kg times 9,990 kPa = 10.1 kJ/kg, against about 1,360 kJ/kg delivered by the turbine. The back work ratio, pump or compressor work divided by turbine work, is under 1 percent. Operating conditions have climbed steadily. Supercritical units run above water’s critical pressure of 22.06 MPa, where there is no boiling plateau at all, and many plants reheat the steam partway through the expansion. Condensers commonly run at about 5 to 10 kPa, where water condenses at 33 to 46 degrees Celsius, depending on the cooling water or air available. Why does an ideal Rankine cycle with steam at 550 degrees Celsius reach only about 41 percent, when the Carnot limit between 550 degrees Celsius and 46 degrees Celsius is 61 percent? The T-s diagram in Figure 2.2 shows the answer. Much of the heat enters while the water is warming as a liquid and while it boils at 311 degrees Celsius, far below the superheat peak. Because q_in = ∫T ds along the constant-pressure heating line, the cycle performs exactly like a Carnot engine operating at the mean temperature of heat addition, T̄_H = q_in/(s3 minus s2). In the worked example below T̄_H is only 540 K (267 degrees Celsius), and the efficiency equals 1 minus T_C/T̄_H. Every classic improvement to steam plants, including higher boiler pressure, reheat, and regenerative feedwater heating with steam bled from the turbine, works by raising T̄_H or lowering T_C. The gas turbine follows the Brayton cycle, named for the American engineer George Brayton, who built constant-pressure combustion engines in the 1870s. Air is compressed, fuel burns in it at nearly constant pressure, and the hot gas expands through a turbine and leaves as exhaust, so the real machine runs an open cycle. For an ideal cycle with air as a perfect gas, efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio r_p: η_B = 1 minus r_p^(minus (kminus 1)/k), where k = c_p/c_v about 1.4. At r_p = 20 this gives 1 minus 20^(minus 0.286) = 57.5 percent. The weak point is the compressor. Compressing a gas takes far more work than pumping a liquid, so even the ideal cycle at r_p = 20 between 288 K and 1,873 K spends 36 percent of the turbine’s work driving its own compressor, and component losses then cut deeply into the net output. That is why gas-turbine progress is measured in firing temperature and component efficiency. Take r_p = 20, air entering at 288 K, a turbine inlet temperature of 1,873 K (1,600 degrees Celsius), isentropic efficiencies of 0.88 for the compressor and 0.90 for the turbine, and c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K). The compressor absorbs 445 kJ/kg, the turbine delivers 974 kJ/kg, and the net 529 kJ/kg divided by the 1,147 kJ/kg of heat added gives 46 percent, with a back work ratio of 0.46 and exhaust leaving at about 630 degrees Celsius. Current heavy-duty H- and J-class machines fire at around 1,600 degrees Celsius, hotter than their nickel-superalloy blades could survive uncooled, and they depend on internal air cooling and ceramic thermal barrier coatings. Real machines also bleed cooling air and lose pressure in ducts, so their simple-cycle efficiencies are lower than this estimate; GE, for example, rates its 60 Hz 7HA.03 at 43.3 percent net (LHV). A common misconception: Our boiler makes steam at 550 degrees Celsius, so the plant is a 550 degrees Celsius heat engine and its efficiency should be close to the Carnot value for 550 degrees Celsius. In fact, Only the last of the heat is added at 550 degrees Celsius. In the ideal cycle at 10 MPa the mean temperature of heat addition is 267 degrees Celsius, so even with no losses the efficiency is 41 percent, not 61 percent. Peak temperature tells you the ceiling; mean temperature tells you the performance.

tracks.label: 2.4 Combined cycles and cogeneration
tracks.text: Section 2 point 4. Combined cycles and cogeneration. Section 2.3 ended with a mismatch. The gas turbine takes in heat at a very high temperature but throws it away hot, at around 600 degrees Celsius. The steam cycle rejects heat close to ambient but takes it in at a low mean temperature. A combined cycle stacks the two. The gas turbine is the topping cycle, and its exhaust flows through a heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG) that raises steam for a Rankine bottoming cycle, as in Figure 2.3. In large plants the HRSG produces steam at three pressure levels, with reheat, so that the water and steam temperatures follow the cooling exhaust closely and less exergy is destroyed in the heat transfer. The plant as a whole then takes in heat at the gas turbine’s high temperatures, from compressor discharge up to the firing temperature, and rejects it near the condenser’s temperature, capturing the best end of each cycle. The combined efficiency follows from a short energy balance. Let the fuel supply heat Q to the gas turbine, which delivers W_B = η_B·Q and rejects (1 minus η_B)·Q in its exhaust. If all of that rejected heat reaches the steam cycle and the steam cycle converts a fraction η_R of it to work, then W_R = η_R(1 minus η_B)·Q. Adding the outputs and dividing by Q gives η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 minus η_B). The relation rests on assumptions worth stating: all heat rejected by the gas turbine is offered to the steam cycle; the steam cycle receives no other heat, so there is no supplementary firing in the HRSG; both efficiencies refer to the same fuel heating value; and auxiliary loads are treated consistently. In practice some exhaust heat escapes through the stack, so η_R is best read as an effective efficiency from exhaust heat to steam-turbine work. This relation explains how combined cycles moved past every other thermal plant. GE rates its 7HA.03 gas turbine at 43.3 percent in simple cycle and at more than 64 percent in combined cycle, both net on a lower-heating-value (LHV) basis. Solving for the bottoming cycle gives η_R = (0.64 minus 0.433)/(1 minus 0.433) = 0.365, so a steam cycle with an effective efficiency of only 36.5 percent adds 21 points. Measured records sit close to such ratings. In 2016 EDF’s Bouchain plant in France, built around a GE 9HA.01, was certified at 62.22 percent net, and in 2018 Chubu Electric’s Nishi-Nagoya Block 1 was recognized at 63.08 percent gross. Fleet averages are lower. U.S. gas combined-cycle units had average tested heat rates of about 7,600 Btu/kWh (HHV) from 2014 to 2021, about 45 percent on that basis (roughly 50 percent LHV); the gap from the ratings comes mainly from the many older, less efficient units in the fleet, with ambient conditions and wear adding to it. Even a combined cycle rejects about a third of its fuel energy as low-temperature heat through its condenser and stack. Cogeneration, or combined heat and power (CHP), uses that heat for industrial process steam, district heating or hot water. The price is electrical output: to deliver useful heat at, say, 120 degrees Celsius, a steam turbine must exhaust at a higher pressure and temperature than a condensing turbine, so each kilogram of steam does less work. CHP performance is often summarized by the utilization factor, ε_u = (W_net + Q_useful)/Q_fuel. Actual cogeneration plants reach utilization factors as high as about 80 percent when there is a steady demand for the heat. That number, however, adds electricity and heat as if a joule of each were equally valuable, which Section 2.1 showed they are not. An exergy view puts CHP on a fair footing. Heat at 120 degrees Celsius has an exergy factor of 1 minus 298.15 K/393.15 K = 0.24. A CHP plant that turns 100 MJ of fuel into 30 MJ of electricity and 50 MJ of useful heat at 120 degrees Celsius has a utilization factor of 80 percent but an exergy efficiency of about (30 + 50 times 0.24)/100 = 42 percent, taking the fuel’s exergy as roughly its heating value. The practical test is the fuel saved compared with making the same products separately. With a 60 percent combined cycle and a 90 percent boiler, separate production takes 30/0.60 + 50/0.90 = 105.6 MJ, so CHP saves only 5 percent. Against a 35 percent coal plant the saving is 1 minus 100/(85.7 + 55.6) = 29 percent. CHP pays most where the electricity it displaces is inefficient and the heat demand is steady. A common misconception: Our CHP plant is 80 percent efficient, so it beats any combined-cycle plant at 60 percent. In fact, The 80 percent is a utilization factor that counts a joule of 120 degrees Celsius heat as equal to a joule of electricity. On an exergy basis that CHP plant is about 42 percent efficient. The fair comparison is fuel use against producing the same electricity and heat separately; against a modern combined cycle and a good boiler, CHP often saves only a few percent.
